# FrontAccounting ERP Migration POC — Summary

**Status:** ✅ POC COMPLETE — Gate 4 passed 2026-03-30

## What it is
A proof-of-concept migration of **FrontAccounting ERP v2.4.19** (PHP 5.6/7.x + MySQL, 133K lines) to a modern stack:
- **Backend:** Python 3.12 + FastAPI + SQLAlchemy 2.x
- **Frontend:** React 18 + TypeScript + shadcn/ui + Tailwind + Vite
- **DB:** PostgreSQL 16
- **Auth:** JWT via FastAPI-Users (replacing PHP `$_SESSION`)
- **Build:** Docker Compose

## Scope completed (5 MWUs)
| MWU | Module | State |
|---|---|---|
| DISC-includes | shared library | Comprehension approved |
| MWU-FA-001 | dimensions (Cost Centres) | Fully validated |
| MWU-FA-002 | taxes | Fully validated |
| MWU-FA-003 | gl (Chart of Accounts) | Fully validated |
| MWU-FA-AUTH | Auth architecture | Planning approved |

## Gate progression
1. **Gate 1** (2026-03-19) — Discovery
2. **Gate 2** (2026-03-25) — Planning (all 5 MWUs)
3. **Gate 3** (2026-03-27) — CodeGen: 63 files, 84 BRs, 74 endpoints
4. **Gate 4** (2026-03-30) — Validation: **285/292 tests passing (97.6%)**, 85/85 BRs

## Key technical decisions
- **Money:** always `Decimal` + canonical `round2()` (never float)
- **Auth:** 15-min access tokens, 7-day refresh, JWT-embedded permissions
- **Multi-company:** MySQL `0_` table prefix → PostgreSQL schemas (`fa_company_N`)
- **Risk flags tracked:** raw SQL in `db_pager.inc`, PG strict-mode GROUP BY, NULL dates, MD5 password migration (90-day deadline)

## What's deferred to Phase 5 (Production Pilot)
- Dual-run vs legacy PHP FA instance
- 7 remaining `TEST_DEFECT` failures (mocks + ECB HTTP)
- `AccountFilters` missing 6 fields (FA-003)
- Exchange variation production fix
- Remaining FA modules: purchasing, sales, inventory, manufacturing, reporting

# `mission-control-demo.html` — Summary

A **single-file, click-through demo** of the "Panasa Modernisation Cockpit" — a fictional dashboard for an AI-agent-driven legacy migration. ~3,000 lines of self-contained HTML/CSS/JS (no build, no external code).

## The story it tells
A demo bank is migrating a **COBOL/CICS monolith → Java 21 + Spring Boot on AWS**. The cockpit walks through migrating one program (`CUST_TXN_BATCH.cbl`) end-to-end. Tagline numbers: **Day 6.2 / 42 estimated · "manual: 540d"** struck through (selling AI speedup).

## The 7-stage pipeline (each click-to-advance)
| Stage | Agent | Headline output |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Discovery | Discovery Agent | 2,847 files · 14 modules indexed |
| 2. Comprehension | Comprehension Agent | 13-entity relationship graph + 247 business rules |
| 3. Planning | Planner Agent | 6-phase strangler-fig plan · 23 PRs |
| 4. Code Generation | CodeGen Agent | 3 Java files · 612 LOC (real COBOL + Java samples embedded) |
| 5. Self Review | Review Agent | **HITL checkpoint** — 12 pass · 3 flagged |
| 6. Testing | Test Agent | 247/248 passing · 94.3% cov · 10k-txn parity replay |
| 7. Merge | Integration Agent | PR #847 merged · blue-green w/ 1% canary |

## UI anatomy
- **Top bar:** brand, engagement target, day counter, live session badge
- **Sub-nav:** Pipeline / Relationships / Artefacts / Agents / Evidence / Audit + live counters
- **Left rail:** the 7 stages with status
- **Canvas (centre):** custom render per stage — including an interactive 13-node relationship graph with click-to-inspect evidence pointers (COBOL paragraph ↔ DB2 table ↔ business rule ↔ Jira ticket)
- **Right column:** Governance panel (parity %, coverage, approvals, 240-module risk grid) + Artefacts list
- **Bottom:** real-time activity log + progress bar / Run+Reset buttons (keyboard: →/Enter/Space advance, R reset)

## Notable demo content baked in
- Real-looking **COBOL source** (`CUST_TXN_BATCH.cbl` w/ `WS-MAX-AMOUNT VALUE 999999.99`) and its **Java port** (`CustomerTransactionBatchService` using `BigDecimal`, `@Service`, `@Transactional`)
- Custom syntax highlighters for both COBOL and Java
- **Evidence pointers** on every claim — file path, line range, snippet (the same "evidence, not assertion" theme as your FrontAccounting POC)
- A "Cap $999,999.99" business rule enforced in COBOL + DB2 check constraint — used to demo cross-evidence traceability

## What it actually does
It's a **scripted demo**, not a real cockpit. Each stage has a hardcoded `dwell` time (2.2–5.2s), pre-baked `doneMeta` strings, fixed artefact lists, and faked governance updates. Click "Run Discovery" → wait → see canned logs scroll → click "Continue" → next stage. Resets cleanly.

## Connection to your other work
The vocabulary maps directly onto your FrontAccounting POC: Discovery/Comprehension/Planning/CodeGen/Review/Test/Merge stages, HITL gates, evidence-linked business rules, governance counters. This looks like the **sales/visual pitch** version of the migration framework you've actually implemented for FA.

Here are some angles, sorted by effort. The core question is: do you want the cockpit to **lead** the story (impression first) or **prove** it (substance first)?

## 1. Re-skin in place (low effort, high payoff)
Swap the Demo Bank/COBOL fixture for the **FA POC's real data**: engagement strip → "FrontAccounting v2.4.19 → Python/FastAPI", code samples → real `dimension_entry.php` + generated FastAPI router, artefacts → your actual files (`output/mkb/...`), numbers → your real 5 MWUs, 84 BRs, 285/292 tests, 97.6% pass. Same chassis, your story. **Biggest credibility win for least work** — and you stop showing prospects a fake bank when you have a real ERP migration.

## 2. Cockpit → Proof handoff (the "trust me / show me" sequence)
Open with the polished, scripted cockpit (60–90 seconds of controlled wow). Then split-screen or hard-cut to a **real terminal + file explorer**: `cat output/logs/audit.jsonl`, open the generated FastAPI module, show `pytest` output. *"That was the story. This is the substrate."* This is the demo a sceptical CTO actually believes.

## 3. Replay mode against real audit log
Make the activity log read from your **real `audit.jsonl`** with timestamps compressed. Day counter ticks Day 0 → Day 6.4 as gates pass. Artefacts populate from actual `output/mkb/` filenames. Looks scripted; *is* historical. Strongest answer to "is this real?" without the risk of a live run.

## 4. Live mode (one small module)
Wire "Run Discovery" to **actually call Claude** against one tiny FA module (e.g. dimensions/ — your simplest). Real streaming output into the activity log. Higher risk (latency, API hiccups) but unforgettable when it lands. Keep a "scripted fallback" toggle for nervous days.

## 5. Prospect-personalised cold open
Before the meeting, swap the engagement strip to *their* name + *their* legacy stack ("Acme Corp · VB6 → .NET 8" or "Globex · Oracle Forms → React"). 15 minutes of prep, but it lands as "they built this for us." Pair with any of the above.

## 6. Lead with governance, not speed
The cockpit's standout feature is **evidence pointers** + HITL checkpoints — and that's the exact story your FA POC tells (Gate 1–4, business rule traceability, audit log, dual-track Discovery). Reframe the demo narrative from *"AI rewrote it fast"* (commoditised pitch) to *"every line is provable, every decision is gated, your auditors will love it"* (your actual differentiator vs Devin/Copilot/etc.). Same demo, different voiceover.

---

**My pick for first version:** #1 + #6 together — re-skin to FA data and frame around governance. About a day's work, and it gives you a demo that's *yours*, not a generic COBOL story. Then add #2 (proof handoff) for technical audiences and #5 (personalisation) for sales meetings.

# Panasa Modernisation Cockpit — FrontAccounting demo

The polished click-through cockpit, re-skinned to walk one real FrontAccounting MWU
(`dimensions/`, MWU-FA-001) end-to-end. The Discovery stage can optionally run a

## What's real right now

- **The source files** in `demo/source/dimensions/` are the actual FrontAccounting v2.4.19 PHP (`add_dimension`, `get_dimension_balance_all`, etc.) — same files your POC analysed.

## What's scripted

| Stage | Reality |
|---|---|
| Comprehension | Relationship graph is hardcoded; click-to-inspect evidence points at real file paths and line ranges in the FA source, but it's not generated live this run |
| Planning | The 6-step sub-task plan is canned |
| Code Generation | The PHP→Python diff shows a *representative* target shape; the proxy is **not** invoking a codegen agent. The Python snippet was hand-shaped to match what your real POC produced |

| Testing | `52 / 53 · 6/6 BRs` is hardcoded — reflects your real POC numbers from CLAUDE.md but isn't running pytest live |
| Merge / Gate 4 | All canned — the "FULLY_VALIDATED" status is from your real POC's `output/workflow/MWU-FA-001.json`, not produced live |
| Day counter, MWU counts, governance | Hardcoded values matching your real CLAUDE.md state |

## What this is, structurally

A **demo skin** sitting on top of your real POC's outputs. The numbers, file paths, business rules, risk flags, reviewer name (Renjith R.), Gate 4 date — all sourced from your actual POC. But the cockpit isn't the pipeline that produced them; your real pipeline ran via PowerShell + separate Claude Code invocations + the audit.jsonl file handoffs described in CLAUDE.md.

## If you want more real

The architecture supports it. To make a second stage live (Comprehension is the natural next), you'd add:
- A second prompt file (`prompt-comprehension.md`)
- A second proxy endpoint (`/comprehension`) that takes Discovery's summary as input
- A `runLiveComprehension(stage)` function in the cockpit, same shape as `runLiveDiscovery`

**Recommendation for customer demos:** keep it scripted-with-one-live-moment. The live Discovery is enough to defeat the "this is just a Figma mockup" objection. The rest being scripted is a *feature* — every demo runs the same, no API outages mid-meeting.

**(a) Live Discovery on the new repo (~2 hours).** Point `SOURCE_DIR` at a different PHP app, generalise `prompt-discovery.md`, keep stages 2–7 scripted. Discovery shows the model actually reading the new code. *Gotcha:* the other 6 stages still talk about `dimensions/`, `add_dimension`, TYPE-EXCEPTION — which will read as fake if a prospect is paying attention. So this only works if you frame the demo as "watch Discovery work, then I'll walk through what the rest of the pipeline does on the FA case study."

**(b) Live Discovery + neutralise stages 2–7 (~half a day).** Same as (a) but I rewrite stages 2–7 to be codebase-agnostic ("here's what Planning does in general", "here's a representative codegen output") rather than pretending to run on a specific repo. Cleaner story, but you lose the punch of seeing the dimensions-specific evidence pointers.

**(c) Actually run the full pipeline end-to-end on the new codebase, generating working FastAPI code (multi-day, real engineering).** This is re-doing your real POC against a fresh app — Discovery, Comprehension, Planning, CodeGen, TestGen, validation, all real, producing a runnable result. 1. **Domain.** Want something **business-y** (invoicing, inventory, simple CRM, expense tracker — like FA's spirit, easy to talk about with prospects), or **utility** (URL shortener, paste bin, file manager — simpler logic, less narrative)? The first lands harder in customer pitches; the second is faster to migrate.

2. **Target stack.** Same as FA POC — **FastAPI + SQLAlchemy 2.x + PostgreSQL + (optional) React**? Or do you want this one in a different target to prove the pipeline's flexibility (e.g. Node/NestJS, Go)? Same stack saves us a week of prompt rework.

Real numbers in hand. Here's the honest comparison:

## Top 3 candidates

| | **shorty** (mikecao) | **PHP-URL-Shortener** (josephdenne) | **Simple-URL-Shortener** (azlux) |
|---|---|---|---|
| LOC | 438 | 200 | 649 |
| PHP files | 3 | 4 | 9 |
| DB style | PDO (parameterized) | mysqli + raw concat | PDO (MySQL or SQLite) |
| Entities | 1 (`urls`) | 1 (`shortenedurls`) | 3 (urls + users + comments) |
| Auth? | No | No | Yes (`login.php`) |
| Business rules | URL hash, hits, IP whitelist, 4 output formats (HTML/XML/JSON/text) | URL validation via curl, IP-restricted, referrals counter | URL CRUD, user history, comments, sessions |
| Last commit | 2011-era class | 2009-era procedural | 2015 (abandoned) |
| Migration story difficulty | LOW — clean PDO ports cleanly | LOW-MED — has SQL concat = real injection migration | MED — multi-entity + auth = closest to FA |
| Demo narrative strength | Good (format negotiation, IP filter) | OK (simplest) | Best (mirrors FA architecture) |

## My recommendation: **shorty**

Why: cleanest pick for *testing the pipeline*. It's class-based and PDO-based (matches modern target idioms), but old enough (2011) to be a real migration. One entity keeps the SQLAlchemy model trivial — which is the right choice when the *goal is testing the pipeline*, not exercising every prompt edge-case. The four-output-format feature gives FastAPI router-design something to do (content negotiation), and `hits`/`accessed` give the parity-test harness something measurable to verify.

**If you want more narrative for prospects:** `azlux/Simple-URL-Shortener` — 3 entities + auth means we get to demonstrate JWT-replaces-PHP-sessions (the exact FA-AUTH story) on a fresh codebase. Costs about 1 extra day, lands harder in a meeting.

**If you want the absolute smallest:** `josephdenne/PHP-URL-Shortener` — 200 LOC. But its raw-SQL-concat style is a different kind of migration challenge (defence: that's actually *useful* for showcasing SQLAlchemy parameterisation, like the FA `db_pager.inc` story).

## Schemas at a glance

**shorty**: `urls(id, url, created, accessed, hits)` — clean.
**PHP-URL-Shortener**: `shortenedurls(id, long_url, created, creator, referrals)` — slightly grungier (`created` as `int(10) unsigned` Unix timestamp, MyISAM engine).
**Simple-URL-Shortener**: URLs + Users + Comments (3 tables, schema created by `installation.php`).

1. Move the clone into `legacymodernisation/migrations/<name>/source/`
2. Set up the workspace skeleton (output dirs, audit.jsonl, etc.)

Reasonable concern, but the realistic risk here is low. Let me break it down honestly:

## What's already happened (zero risk)
Cloning + reading the source is just text on disk. `git clone` of a public repo doesn't execute anything. Reading PHP files with Claude is reading. No vector. Your laptop is fine.

## What hasn't happened yet (where actual risk lives)
**Running the PHP code** is where you'd take any risk — and only for option (iii)'s dual-run step. Even then, the risk is small and easily mitigated:
- **Don't expose to the internet.** Run PHP bound to `localhost` only (`php -S 127.0.0.1:8080`) or inside Docker with no port forwarding to 0.0.0.0. Zero external attack surface.
- **No host mounts beyond source.** Docker container reads `source/` and writes a SQLite/MySQL volume — can't touch your filesystem.
- **No `composer install` needed.** All 4 of these repos are framework-less plain PHP — no dependency chain to worry about (composer/npm supply-chain attacks are the real laptop-infection vector for open-source projects, and none of these have it).

The "I run unknown PHP on my Mac" risk in practice is close to zero unless your PHP is months out of date AND someone on your LAN is hostile AND you bind to `0.0.0.0`. Not a realistic threat model.

## Per-repo code-quality notes (these affect *the migration story*, not your laptop)

- **shorty** — clean PDO with bound parameters. No obvious vulnerabilities. Probably the safest to run.
- **Simple-URL-Shortener** (azlux) — PDO, last touched 2015. Auth code likely has weak password handling (MD5 era). Same kind of code-smell as FA — actually good for the migration story.
- **PHP-URL-Shortener** (josephdenne) — **has actual SQL injection patterns** (string-concatenated queries despite `mysqli_real_escape_string`). Uses `get_magic_quotes_gpc()` which was removed in PHP 7. **Don't run as-is on anything reachable**, but it's *interesting* for the migration story — these are exactly the kinds of vulns the FastAPI migration eliminates.
- **simple-guestbook** — too small to evaluate seriously; probably fine.

## Recommended posture

1. **Discovery/Comprehension/Planning/CodeGen** — pure analysis, no execution. Zero risk.
2. **Test execution** — pytest on the generated FastAPI code runs in your normal Python env. Standard dev risk (i.e. minimal).
3. **Dual-run vs PHP** — run the PHP version inside a Docker container, network bound to `127.0.0.1` only. I'll write the Dockerfile/compose so it's locked down by default. No host port mapping to public interfaces, ephemeral DB volume.

If you want belt-and-suspenders: do the dual-run on a VM, or skip the dual-run step (do parity tests by replaying recorded fixtures instead of running both apps live). You still get the migration story; you just verify against captured PHP output instead of live PHP.

## Bottom line

- Cloning + analyzing: do it without thinking twice.
- Running PHP locally in Docker bound to loopback: standard dev hygiene, not laptop-infection-grade risk.
- Choice of repo doesn't change your laptop's risk — only changes what kind of code-smell story the migration tells.

The key analysis points I've gathered:

**encode/decode/get_seed triplet analysis:**
- `get_seed(n, salt, padding)`: computes `md5(n + salt)`, takes first `padding` hex chars, converts to decimal, mods by `10^padding`, clamps to minimum 1, zero-pads to `padding` digits. Returns a `padding`-length decimal string.
- `encode(n)`: if salt+padding active, concatenates seed string with `n` as string then casts to int: `(int)($k . $n)`. So for id=5, salt="abc", padding=3, if seed="042", n becomes `(int)"0425"` = 425. Then passes to `num_to_alpha`.
- `decode(s)`: converts back to number via `alpha_to_num`, then `substr($n, $padding)` strips the leading `padding` digits.
- `num_to_alpha`: base-62 encoding (base = len($chars)), most-significant-digit first.
- `alpha_to_num`: base-62 decoding.

**Important edge cases:**
- When padding=0 OR salt is empty, encoding is pure base-62 of the ID integer — no obfuscation.
- `decode` returns `substr($n, $this->padding)` — this is string `substr` on the integer result of `alpha_to_num`. PHP treats the int as a string when passed to `substr`. So if decoded number is `4251` and padding=3, result is "1" → which then goes to `fetch("1")`. This means the decode path relies on string operations on numeric values.
- The seed guarantees the padding prefix is always non-zero (clamped to minimum 1), so `str_pad` works correctly and `(int)` cast doesn't lose leading zeros (they're still stripped later by `substr`).
- URL stability guarantee: same `(id, salt, padding, chars)` tuple always produces same short code. Migration must preserve all four values exactly.

## FrontAccounting POC — Per-Stage Prompt Structure Enumeration

---

### **Overview: Six-Stage Pipeline with HITL Gates**

The FA migration POC implements a **linear six-stage pipeline** (Discovery → Comprehension → Planning → CodeGen → Self-Review → TestGen) orchestrated by a central Orchestrator Agent that enforces a state machine with human-in-the-loop (HITL) gates between phases. Below is the canonical prompt structure per stage.

---

### **1. DISCOVERY STAGE**

**Canonical prompt:** `/prompts/mwu-fa-001-discovery-01.md` (dimensions/ module — cleanest generic example)

**Structure:**
- POC Mode Override (Track A vs B explanation)
- Task (module name, phase, complexity via semgrep pre-analysis)
- Target stack declaration
- FA-Specific Discovery Rules (6 rules: table prefix `0_`, `*_db.inc` layer, `$_SESSION` ref tagging, `include()` mapping, monetary arithmetic flagging, PostgreSQL GROUP BY/LIMIT/OFFSET compatibility, type mapping)
- Embedded source files (PHP, DDL, includes)
- No external tool calls (READ-ONLY, inline sources)

**Output:** `{module}/track-a/discovery-001.md`

**FA-specific markers:** `TB_PREF` constant, `db_escape()` calls, `ST_DIMENSION` constants, `DECIMAL-REVIEW`, `JWT-REDESIGN`, `PG-STRICT-MODE`, `PG-LIMIT-OFFSET` flags

**Reusable structure:** Section headings (Rules, Pre-Analysis, Source Files) are generic; discovery rules are FA-specific but pattern-transferable to other PHP+MySQL systems

**Approval status:** No explicit marker in prompt; agent invocation moved to `DISCOVERY_HITL` state for human review

---

### **2. COMPREHENSION STAGE**

**Canonical prompt:** `/prompts/mwu-fa-001-comprehension-01.md`

**Structure:**
- Role statement (extract business intent, not just code mechanics)
- Output path + workflow audit log append instruction
- Additional Context to Read (4 dependencies: discovery-001.md, ui-inventory.md, auth architecture-001.md, function-index.md)
- Source files embedded in full
- Comprehension principles (infer intent, consolidate facets, resolve code-vs-docs conflicts, write testable rules, capture edge cases)

**Output:** `{module}/comprehension-001.md`  
**Audit log entry:** `INVOCATION_COMPLETE` event with `state: COMPREHENSION_RUNNING`

**FA-specific:** Dependencies on `$Refs->save()`, `add_comments()`, cross-module stub contracts (CommentsService, RefsService)

**Approval status:** Agent transitions to `COMPREHENSION_HITL`; human validates business rule catalog

---

### **3. PLANNING STAGE** (Only MWU-FA-003 has explicit planning prompt)

**Canonical prompt:** `/prompts/mwu-fa-003-planning-01.md`

### What is shorty?

Shorty is a self-hosted, single-file PHP URL shortener authored by Mike Cao (MIT licence, 2011). It accepts a long URL via a query-string parameter, stores it in a single MySQL `urls` table, and returns a short alphanumeric code derived from the auto-incremented row ID. Subsequent requests using that short code are resolved with a permanent HTTP 301 redirect back to the original URL. The code is entirely contained in one class (`Shorty`, `shorty.php`), one bootstrap (`index.php`), and one config file (`config.php`). There is no framework, no auth layer, no queue, and no cache — it is a minimal, stateless PHP script.

### Why migrate?

The source stack (PHP 5.x / MySQL / Apache mod_rewrite) is end-of-life. The target organisation is standardising on Python 3.12 + FastAPI + PostgreSQL 16, and this codebase is selected as the pilot migration unit precisely because of its low complexity: single entity, clean PDO, no sessions, no money fields, no complex joins. A successful migration here validates the pipeline (Discovery → Comprehension → Planning → CodeGen → Self-Review → TestGen → Dual-run → Gate 4) before it is applied to the larger FrontAccounting ERP.

### Complexity Rating

**LOW.** Rationale: single database table, single class (~395 lines), zero external library dependencies, no authentication, no monetary arithmetic, no multi-tenancy, no batch operations. 11	### What is shorty?
12	
13	Shorty is a self-hosted, single-file PHP URL shortener authored by Mike Cao (MIT licence, 2011). It accepts a long URL via a query-string parameter, stores it in a single MySQL `urls` table, and returns a short alphanumeric code derived from the auto-incremented row ID. Subsequent requests using that short code are resolved with a permanent HTTP 301 redirect back to the original URL. The code is entirely contained in one class (`Shorty`, `shorty.php`), one bootstrap (`index.php`), and one config file (`config.php`). There is no framework, no auth layer, no queue, and no cache — it is a minimal, stateless PHP script.

16

The target organisation is standardising on Python 3.12 + FastAPI + PostgreSQL 16, and this codebase is selected as the pilot migration unit precisely because of its low complexity: single entity, clean PDO, no sessions, no money fields, no complex joins. 11	### What is shorty?
12	
13	Shorty is a self-hosted, single-file PHP URL shortener authored by Mike Cao (MIT licence, 2011). It accepts a long URL via a query-string parameter, stores it in a single MySQL `urls` table, and returns a short alphanumeric code derived from the auto-incremented row ID. Subsequent requests using that short code are resolved with a permanent HTTP 301 redirect back to the original URL. The code is entirely contained in one class (`Shorty`, `shorty.php`), one bootstrap (`index.php`), and one config file (`config.php`). There is no framework, no auth layer, no queue, and no cache — it is a minimal, stateless PHP script.
14	
15	### Why migrate?
16	
17	The source stack (PHP 5.x / MySQL / Apache mod_rewrite) is end-of-life. The target organisation is standardising on Python 3.12 + FastAPI + PostgreSQL 16, and this codebase is selected as the pilot migration unit precisely because of its low complexity: single entity, clean PDO, no sessions, no money fields, no complex joins. A successful migration here validates the pipeline (Discovery → Comprehension → Planning → CodeGen → Self-Review → TestGen → Dual-run → Gate 4) before it is applied to the larger FrontAccounting ERP.

26	from typing import Any

28	_LOG_FORMAT = "%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s %(message)s"
29	_DATE_FORMAT = "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z"

31	
32	class _JsonFormatter(logging.Formatter):
33	    """Single-line JSON output for structured ingestion."""
34	
35	    def format(self, record: logging.LogRecord) -> str:
36	        payload: dict[str, Any] = {
37	            "ts": self.formatTime(record, _DATE_FORMAT),
38	            "level": record.levelname,
39	            "logger": record.name,
40	            "msg": record.getMessage(),
41	        }
42	        # Attach any structured extras the caller passed via `extra=`.
43	        for key, value in record.__dict__.items():
44	            if key in (
45	                "args", "msg", "levelname", "levelno", "pathname", "filename",
46	                "module", "exc_info", "exc_text", "stack_info", "lineno",
47	                "funcName", "created", "msecs", "relativeCreated", "thread",
48	                "threadName", "processName", "process", "name",
49	            ):
50	                continue
51	            payload[key] = value
52	        if record.exc_info:
53	            payload["exc"] = self.formatException(record.exc_info)
54	        return json.dumps(payload, default=str)

57	def configure_logging(level: str = "INFO", json_logs: bool = False) -> None:
58	    """Install handlers on the root logger.
59	
60	    Idempotent — repeated calls remove any previously attached handlers
61	    before installing a fresh one.

-- IDENTICAL known rows so the parity-runner can compare lookup behaviour against
-- pre-existing URLs in addition to create-new-URL behaviour.

-- separately (different INSERT syntax + DEFAULT now() handling).

-- IMPORTANT: id values are explicitly set. They must match across both DBs so the
-- encoded short codes are stable for parity comparison.

CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS shorty
  CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;
USE shorty;

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS urls (
    id        INT UNSIGNED NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,
    url       VARCHAR(1000) NOT NULL,
    created   DATETIME NOT NULL,
    accessed  DATETIME,
    hits      INT UNSIGNED NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    PRIMARY KEY (id),
    UNIQUE (url)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

--   id=999          → 3-digit boundary

12	### 1.1 Layered architecture (models / schemas / service / router / encode-module)
13	
14	The target follows the FrontAccounting POC's established `app/modules/<feature>/` convention. Bad input.

` (legacy mod_php quirk) - New: http://127.0.0.1:18000/?url=ftp://invalid → 400 with `{"detail":"Bad input.","type":"shorty/bad-input"}` (proper HTTP) This is the documented status-code uplift from RF-09 — the migration *fixed* it. **FastAPI extras:** - http://127.0.0.1:18000/docs — auto-generated OpenAPI Swagger UI (the new app comes with this for free; legacy doesn't) - http://127.0.0.1:18000/healthz — liveness probe (returns JSON, useful for k8s) **The parity proof (machine-readable):** - File: `migrations/shorty/dual-run/reports/parity-report.json` — 466 lines · summary: 14 PASS · 0 FAIL · 6 documented divergences · green-path 9/9 (100%) ## To stop / restart everything ``` cd migrations/shorty/dual-run docker compose ps # current state docker compose down # stop (keeps volumes) docker compose down -v # stop + wipe DB data docker compose up -d # bring it all back ``` The cockpit playback is still on http://localhost:3737/shorty/ (proxy from earlier).

You're right — that's an accurate observation, and it's a feature of *what shorty actually is*, not a bug in the demo. ## Why there's no visual delta shorty is **a backend-only API** by design — no HTML forms, no admin panel, no JS UI. Its entire surface is `GET /?url=…` and `GET /`. So both the legacy and the new render exactly the same thing in a browser: an `…` anchor or raw JSON. The migration moved everything that matters (encoding, DB, error handling, observability, test coverage, type safety, ProxyHeaders, OpenAPI contract) but none of it shows up in a browser tab. **For a backend-only app, "visual proof of migration" = test reports + parity report + the new Swagger UI**. The one already-existing visual delta you can see right now: open http://127.0.0.1:18000/docs — that's the FastAPI auto-generated **Swagger / OpenAPI** UI, listing all 5 endpoints with try-it-out forms and JSON schemas. The legacy has no equivalent. Migration produces visible-UI delta for free. Doesn't help this engagement, but worth knowing for the next one. My recommendation: **(a)**. ## Key Best Practices

### Async Engine and Session Setup
Use `create_async_engine` and `AsyncSession` for non-blocking database access. Use SQLAlchemy 2.0+ with asyncpg for PostgreSQL async support, as asyncpg is the recommended driver for SQLAlchemy's asynchronous PostgreSQL backend.

### SERIAL INTEGER Handling
When creating tables, SQLAlchemy will issue the SERIAL datatype for integer-based primary key columns, which generates a sequence and server side default corresponding to the column. This is handled automatically by SQLAlchemy when you define integer primary keys.

### Connection Pool Configuration
Configure connection pooling with pool_size, max_overflow, pool_timeout, and pool_recycle settings for production workloads.

### Async-First Design
For new projects, reach for SQLAlchemy 2.0's async API (AsyncSession, async_sessionmaker). Configure connection pools based on your workload and database limits, use dependency injection for clean session lifecycle management, and choose the right loading strategy to avoid N+1 queries.

### Query Optimization
Use `add_all` for bulk inserts and streaming for large result sets to reduce memory usage.

### Session Dependency Management
Use FastAPI dependency injection (get_db) to ensure proper session lifecycle management (creation and closing).

The stack combines FastAPI's async capabilities with SQLAlchemy 2.0's async ORM to handle thousands of concurrent database operations efficiently without blocking the event loop.

11	## §1. Engagement Context
12	
13	### What is chapagain/crud-php-simple?
14	
15	chapagain/crud-php-simple is a minimal, educational PHP CRUD application written in classic procedural style against a single MySQL `users` table with four columns: `id`, `name`, `age`, and `email`. The entire codebase is 222 lines across seven PHP files, one SQL DDL script, and a README. It implements four distinct screens — a record list, an add form, an edit form, and a direct-delete handler — using bare HTML 3.2-era markup (`<table border=0 bgcolor='#DDDDDD'>`, `<font color='red'>`) with no CSS framework, no templating layer, and no MVC separation. Database access is handled via the `mysqli_*` procedural extension with inline SQL strings. It was published as a blog-post companion piece illustrating the simplest possible PHP CRUD, and as such it makes no attempt at production hardening: there are no CSRF tokens, no input type validation, minimal XSS protection, and two confirmed SQL injection vectors. It is exactly the kind of file-per-page PHP legacy that enterprises accumulated between 1999 and 2010 and that modernisation pipelines exist to replace.
16	
17	### Why migrate?
18	
19	The application has multiple critical security vulnerabilities that would be unacceptable in any customer-facing or internal-production deployment: two direct SQL injection vectors (`edit.php` and `delete.php` both use unescaped GET parameters directly in SQL), stored XSS via unescaped column values echoed into HTML, and no CSRF protection on any mutating operation. Beyond security, the user experience is trapped in the 1990s — four separate full-page navigations for simple CRUD, JavaScript `window.confirm()` for delete confirmation, and `<font>` tags for error feedback. The target stack (FastAPI + React 18 + shadcn/ui + Tailwind) replaces all of this with a single-page application offering a modern DataTable, modal-driven add/edit flows, an AlertDialog for delete confirmation, and Toast notifications — delivering a visually compelling "old vs new" contrast that is the primary demo artefact for this engagement.
20	
21	### Complexity rating: LOW
22	
23	Rationale: one table, four columns, four operations (CRUD), no joins, no transactions, no business logic beyond empty-field validation, no authentication, no multi-tenancy, no file uploads, no pagination. The complexity of this migration lies entirely in the security remediations and the UI transformation, not in business logic fidelity. The backend API surface is five endpoints (list, create, read-one, update, delete). The React SPA is one route with two modals and one alert dialog.

11	## §1. Engagement Context
12	
13	### What is chapagain/crud-php-simple?
14	
15	chapagain/crud-php-simple is a minimal, educational PHP CRUD application written in classic procedural style against a single MySQL `users` table with four columns: `id`, `name`, `age`, and `email`. The entire codebase is 222 lines across seven PHP files, one SQL DDL script, and a README. It implements four distinct screens — a record list, an add form, an edit form, and a direct-delete handler — using bare HTML 3.2-era markup (`<table border=0 bgcolor='#DDDDDD'>`, `<font color='red'>`) with no CSS framework, no templating layer, and no MVC separation. Database access is handled via the `mysqli_*` procedural extension with inline SQL strings. It was published as a blog-post companion piece illustrating the simplest possible PHP CRUD, and as such it makes no attempt at production hardening: there are no CSRF tokens, no input type validation, minimal XSS protection, and two confirmed SQL injection vectors. It is exactly the kind of file-per-page PHP legacy that enterprises accumulated between 1999 and 2010 and that modernisation pipelines exist to replace.
16	
17	### Why migrate?
18	
19	The application has multiple critical security vulnerabilities that would be unacceptable in any customer-facing or internal-production deployment: two direct SQL injection vectors (`edit.php` and `delete.php` both use unescaped GET parameters directly in SQL), stored XSS via unescaped column values echoed into HTML, and no CSRF protection on any mutating operation. Beyond security, the user experience is trapped in the 1990s — four separate full-page navigations for simple CRUD, JavaScript `window.confirm()` for delete confirmation, and `<font>` tags for error feedback. The target stack (FastAPI + React 18 + shadcn/ui + Tailwind) replaces all of this with a single-page application offering a modern DataTable, modal-driven add/edit flows, an AlertDialog for delete confirmation, and Toast notifications — delivering a visually compelling "old vs new" contrast that is the primary demo artefact for this engagement.
20	
21	### Complexity rating: LOW
22	
23	Rationale: one table, four columns, four operations (CRUD), no joins, no transactions, no business logic beyond empty-field validation, no authentication, no multi-tenancy, no file uploads, no pagination. The complexity of this migration lies entirely in the security remediations and the UI transformation, not in business logic fidelity. The backend API surface is five endpoints (list, create, read-one, update, delete). The React SPA is one route with two modals and one alert dialog.

This engagement migrates `chapagain/crud-php-simple` to a **two-codebase modern stack**: a Python 3.12 + FastAPI 0.110 + SQLAlchemy 2.x async + PostgreSQL 16 service, and a React 18 + TypeScript SPA wrapping shadcn/ui primitives. The two halves communicate exclusively over five JSON HTTP endpoints under the `/api/users` prefix; nothing else crosses the boundary. There is no server-side rendering, no shared template, no PHP-style mixed-mode response — the API returns Pydantic-serialised JSON, and React owns every pixel of the UI. This is the first of the three engagements that ships a frontend codebase alongside the backend, so the plan below treats the React tree as a first-class peer of the FastAPI tree, with its own layer firewall, its own test plan, and its own role in the dual-run screenshot harness.

### 1.1 Backend layers (models / schemas / service / router)

The backend mirrors the shorty engagement's proven four-layer split. From innermost to outermost:

- **Model layer** (`app/modules/users/models.py`) — SQLAlchemy 2.x `DeclarativeBase` subclass with `Mapped[T]` typed columns. Owns persistence concerns and constraint declarations (`UniqueConstraint`, `CheckConstraint`). Imports only from `sqlalchemy` and the local `app.db.base.Base`. Never imports FastAPI, never imports Pydantic.
- **Schema layer** (`app/modules/users/schemas.py`) — Pydantic v2 DTOs (`UserBase`, `UserCreate`, `UserUpdate`, `UserRead`, `ProblemDetail`, `HealthResponse`). These are the wire contract; tests assert against these field-for-field. No SQLAlchemy types leak into a schema; no `Mapped[T]` annotations appear here.
- **Service layer** (`app/modules/users/service.py`) — `UserService` class with five async public methods (`list_users`, `create_user`, `get_user`, `update_user`, `delete_user`). Receives an `AsyncSession` per call from the router. Raises domain exceptions defined in `errors.py` (`UserNotFound`, `EmailAlreadyExists`). Owns the BR-C-11 IntegrityError→409 translation. **No FastAPI imports**, no `HTTPException`, no `Request`/`Response` — this preserves unit-testability against a hand-rolled `AsyncSession`.
- **Router layer** (`app/modules/users/router.py`) — FastAPI `APIRouter` declaring the five endpoints. Wires `Depends(get_session)` + `Depends(get_user_service)`. Catches domain exceptions and returns `JSONResponse` with the `ProblemDetail` envelope. Does **not** import from `sqlalchemy` directly — the only SQL surface is via `UserService`.

A separate **errors module** (`app/modules/users/errors.py`) defines the domain exception hierarchy. A separate **dependencies module** (`app/modules/users/dependencies.py`) owns the `get_user_service()` provider and the `init_user_service(settings)` lifespan-bound bootstrapper.

### 1.2 Frontend layers (pages / components / hooks / api client / types)

The frontend uses a five-layer split with strict directional dependencies. Each layer may only import from layers below it:

1. **Pages** (`src/pages/`) — top-level route handlers. For this engagement: a single `UsersPage`. Pages own ephemeral UI state (modal open/close, currently-selected user) via `useState`. Pages compose components.
2. **Components** (`src/components/`) — presentational + interactive UI primitives wrapping shadcn/ui. Five custom components plus shadcn-generated primitives that get copied into `src/components/ui/`. Components are pure props-in / events-out; they never call the API directly.
3. **Hooks** (`src/hooks/`) — TanStack React Query wrappers (`useUsersQuery`, `useCreateUser`, `useUpdateUser`, `useDeleteUser`). Hooks own server state, cache keys, and mutation lifecycle (`onSuccess` invalidation, `onError` toast plumbing). Hooks call the API client.
4. **API client** (`src/api/`) — typed `fetch` wrappers. One function per endpoint. Translates RFC-9457 `ProblemDetail` envelopes into typed errors. Owns the `VITE_API_BASE` lookup.
5. **Lib / types** (`src/lib/`, `src/types/`) — pure utilities: Zod schemas, the User TypeScript type, the ProblemDetail parser, the className `cn()` helper that shadcn installs. No React, no fetch, no state.

1	# MWU-CRUD-001 — Planning Report
2	
3	**Classification:** APPROVED-CANDIDATE (awaits Gate 3)
4	**Generated:** 2026-05-14
5	**Agent:** planner_agent (Opus · code-architect)
6	**Upstream:** comprehension-001.md · gate-1.md · gate-2.md
7	
8	---
9	
10	## 1. Architecture overview
11	
12	Two-codebase migration: Python 3.12 + FastAPI 0.110 + SQLAlchemy 2.x async + PostgreSQL 16 (backend) and React 18 + TypeScript + shadcn/ui + Tailwind + Vite + TanStack Query (frontend). Communication via five JSON HTTP endpoints under `/api/users`. No SSR, no shared templates — clean API ↔ SPA boundary.
13	
14	### 1.1 Backend layers (4-tier, mirrors shorty's proven split)
15	
16	- **Model** (`app/modules/users/models.py`) — SQLAlchemy `DeclarativeBase`, `Mapped[T]`, constraints. Imports only `sqlalchemy` + `app.db.base.Base`. No FastAPI, no Pydantic.
17	- **Schema** (`app/modules/users/schemas.py`) — Pydantic v2 DTOs. The wire contract. No SQLAlchemy.
18	- **Service** (`app/modules/users/service.py`) — `UserService` class, 5 async methods, raises domain exceptions. NO FastAPI imports.
19	- **Router** (`app/modules/users/router.py`) — `APIRouter`, `Depends`, catches domain exceptions → `ProblemDetail`. Does NOT import sqlalchemy except `AsyncSession` as a type.
20	
21	Plus `errors.py` (`UsersError`, `UserNotFound`, `EmailAlreadyExists`) and `dependencies.py` (`get_user_service`, `init_user_service`).
22	
23	### 1.2 Frontend layers (5-tier, strict downward imports)
24	
25	1. **Pages** (`src/pages/`) — `UsersPage`. Owns ephemeral UI state via `useState`. Composes components.
26	2. **Components** (`src/components/`) — presentational + interactive, wrap shadcn primitives. Pure props-in / events-out. Never call API directly.
27	3. **Hooks** (`src/hooks/`) — TanStack Query wrappers. Own server state, cache keys, mutation lifecycle.
28	4. **API client** (`src/api/`) — typed fetch wrappers. Translates RFC-9457 envelopes. Owns `VITE_API_BASE`.
29	5. **Lib / types** (`src/lib/`, `src/types/`) — pure utilities. No React, no fetch.
30	
31	### 1.3 Layer firewall (non-negotiable)
32	
33	| Firewall | Enforcement |
34	|---|---|
35	| `service.py` ≠ `from fastapi/starlette` | grep returns zero |
36	| `router.py` ≠ `from sqlalchemy` (except `AsyncSession` typing) | All SQL via UserService |
37	| `models.py` ≠ `from fastapi/pydantic` | Persistence decoupled |
38	| `schemas.py` ≠ `from sqlalchemy` | Wire decoupled |
39	| Components ≠ `from "@/api/"` directly | Always via hooks |
40	| `src/lib/` & `src/types/` ≠ React imports | Pure, testable, tree-shakeable |
41	| `src/api/` ≠ React imports | Plain fetch, vitest+msw-friendly |
42	
43	### 1.4 Async + Pydantic v2 + SQLAlchemy 2.x conventions
44	
45	- Every route + service method `async def`. No sync paths.
46	- Engine: `create_async_engine("postgresql+asyncpg://...", pool_pre_ping=True)`.
47	- Sessions: `async_sessionmaker(engine, expire_on_commit=False, class_=AsyncSession)`.
48	- `Mapped[T]` + `mapped_column(...)` only.
49	- Pydantic v2: `ConfigDict(from_attributes=True, str_strip_whitespace=True)` for response; `ConfigDict(extra="forbid")` for request.
50	- `model_dump()`, `model_validate()`, `EmailStr` (requires `pydantic[email]`).
51	- Queries via `select(...)`, `update(...)`, `delete(...)` — no raw SQL strings.
52	
53	### 1.5 Frontend toolchain (locked)
54	
55	| Layer | Choice | Version |
56	|---|---|---|
57	| Build | Vite | 5.x |
58	| Language | TypeScript (strict) | 5.x |
59	| UI runtime | React | 18.x |
60	| Components | shadcn/ui (Radix + Tailwind) | latest |
61	| Styling | Tailwind CSS | 3.x |
62	| Server state | TanStack Query | v5 |
63	| Forms | react-hook-form + @hookform/resolvers | latest |
64	| Client validation | Zod | 3.x |
65	| Table | @tanstack/react-table (via shadcn DataTable wrapper) | 8.x |
66	| Test runner | Vitest + Testing Library | latest |
67	| Mock server | MSW | 2.x |
68	
69	NOT introduced (Gate-2 lock): Redux, Zustand, Next.js, React Router (single route), styled-components, axios.
70

38	keep **UserCreation** and **UserUpdate** distinct rather than merging them into a single
39	"UserMutation" — they share schema but diverge on (a) identifier (Create=none, Update=path `id`),
40	(b) HTTP verb (POST vs PUT), (c) success status (201 vs 200), and (d) error surface (Create can

47	| **UserCreation** | Add a new user record honouring all required-field, type-range, format, and uniqueness invariants. | `POST /api/users` | BR-C-03, BR-C-04, BR-C-05, BR-C-06, BR-C-11 |

# Panasa Modernisation Cockpit — FrontAccounting demo

The polished click-through cockpit, re-skinned to walk one real FrontAccounting MWU
(`dimensions/`, MWU-FA-001) end-to-end. The Discovery stage can optionally run a
**real** Claude call against the embedded PHP source and stream findings into the
activity log.

## Two modes

| Mode | URL | What runs | Needs API key? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Scripted** (default) | `http://localhost:3737/` | All 7 stages canned, deterministic | No |
| **Live (Discovery)** | `http://localhost:3737/?live=true` | Discovery streams from Claude; stages 2–7 stay scripted | Yes |

The live-mode hand-off is invisible to a viewer: if the proxy is unreachable
or the SSE stream stalls, the cockpit silently falls back to the scripted
Discovery timeline — the demo never gets stuck.

## One-time setup

```bash
cd demo/proxy
npm install
cp .env.example .env
# edit .env and paste your ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
```

## Run the demo

```bash
cd demo/proxy
npm start
# → [cockpit-proxy] listening on http://localhost:3737
```

Then open one of:

- **Scripted only** — `http://localhost:3737/`
- **Live Discovery** — `http://localhost:3737/?live=true`

Click **Run Discovery** (or press `→`). Reset with `R` between runs.

## What "live" actually does

1. Browser opens an SSE connection to `GET /discovery`.
2. The proxy reads every `.php` / `.inc` file under `demo/source/dimensions/`
   (9 files, ~750 LOC) and embeds them into the prompt at
   `proxy/prompt-discovery.md`.
3. Proxy calls `claude-sonnet-4-6` with `messages.stream` and forwards
   model output, **line by line**, with a strict regex filter:
   `^\[DISCOVERY\] .{8,200}$`. Anything that doesn't match (preamble, code
   fences, stray prose) is silently dropped.
4. The model also emits a final JSON summary block. The proxy parses it and
   sends a `summary` SSE event; the cockpit uses it to populate the
   `doneMeta` line, governance counters, and the artefact list.

End-to-end latency: ~25–40 seconds for ~18 findings + summary.

# Dual-run PHP side — runs unmodified chapagain/crud-php-simple against MySQL 8.
# Build context = migration root (../); we COPY both source/ and the overlay.

FROM php:8.2-apache

RUN docker-php-ext-install mysqli
RUN printf '<Directory /var/www/html>\n  AllowOverride All\n  Require all granted\n</Directory>\n' \
    > /etc/apache2/conf-enabled/crud.conf

WORKDIR /var/www/html

# Bake legacy source + container-aware dbConnection.php into the image.
COPY source/ /var/www/html/
COPY dual-run/php-overlay/dbConnection.php /var/www/html/dbConnection.php

EXPOSE 80

# PNS-CRUD-001 — engagement-specific learnings

## What this run validated vs prior engagements

This was the third pipeline run and the **first with a frontend codegen arm**. Prior engagements (FA POC, shorty) proved the backend half. This run proved:

- **The visual artefact is load-bearing.** "Old vs new" screenshots are what customers actually internalise — the table-border=0 → shadcn DataTable mosaic at `screenshots/mosaic.png` is more persuasive than any test count. Customer prospects don't care about 107/107 tests; they care that the bare HTML form turned into the validated Radix dialog.
- **One entity is enough.** `users` (4 columns, 222 PHP LOC) was small enough to fit in a single Planning doc and big enough to exercise every layer firewall, every shadcn primitive, every error envelope. Anything smaller would have been a toy; anything bigger would have hidden the wiring.

## Real defects caught (in order of stage that found them)

| # | Stage | File:line | Class of bug |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Self-Review | `config.py:53` | pydantic-settings alias + env_prefix double-prefix (silent env-var fail) |
| 2 | Self-Review | `UsersPage.tsx:165` | `JSX.Element` deprecated in TS 5.x + react-jsx transform — breaks `tsc --noEmit` |
| 3 | TestGen | `UserForm.tsx:67` | early-return on `errors.length === 0` short-circuits the 409→email projection |
| 4–11 | Dual-run | docker-compose + Dockerfiles + seeds | 8 integration-layer mismatches (see below) |

**The 11-fix tally is the pipeline's value, not a flaw.** Each defect was caught at the stage designed to catch that class.

## What only manifested at container boundary

Pure static review (Stage 5) + unit/integration tests (Stage 6) **could not have caught**:

- `CRUD_DB_URL` vs `CRUD_DATABASE_URL` — Settings reads `env_prefix + field_name`; compose used the wrong name. Tests pass because conftest builds Settings in-process.
- `http://api:8000` vs `http://fastapi-new:8000` — nginx upstream pointed at a service that doesn't exist. Vite dev server hides this; only the production nginx build exposes it.
- `/healthz` vs `/api/healthz` — healthcheck path mismatched the mounted API prefix.
- `crud-mysql` vs `mysql-legacy` — PHP overlay referenced the wrong compose service.
- `VITE_API_BASE_URL` vs `VITE_API_BASE` — frontend reads one name, compose set the other. Defaulted to `/api` which happened to work after nginx fix.

**Generalisable learning for this stack:** any service name appearing in nginx/compose/healthcheck/env-var/source code is a coupling point. A single "names of things" lookup table at the top of `docker-compose.yml` (or a `.env` file consumed by both sides) would have prevented 5 of 11 fixes.

## Library-specific gotchas surfaced

1. **Pydantic `EmailStr` rejects `.test` TLD** per RFC 2606. Seed data using `alice@example.test` failed UserRead validation at `/api/users` — `eve@example.test` → 500 from `model_validate`. The community convention "use `.test` for tests" doesn't survive an email library that follows IANA reserved lists. **Use `.com` / `.io` in fixtures.**

2. **pydantic-settings JSON-decodes complex env-var values BEFORE running `@field_validator(mode="before")`**. The CSV-parsing validator in `config.py:77-83` is unreachable from env vars. Workaround was to pass `CRUD_CORS_ORIGINS` as a JSON array literal in compose. **Implication: for any `list[str]` or `dict` field that's intended to come from env, either pass JSON or override `parse_env_var()`.**

3. **TanStack Query v5.20 changed mutation `onSuccess` from 3-arg to 4-arg.** CodeGen wrote `(data, variables, context)` patterns that satisfied vitest (which doesn't run tsc) but failed `tsc --noEmit` during `npm run build` inside docker. **Vitest passing ≠ build passing.** Switched all 3 hooks to `(...args)` rest forwarding to be signature-agnostic across future TanStack versions.

4. **The Playwright Python base image ships browsers but not the `playwright` Python package itself.** Counterintuitive, but verified — had to add `playwright==1.47.0` to the runner's pip install.

## Layer-firewall behaviour under test

The "service ≠ fastapi imports / router ≠ direct sqlalchemy / components ≠ direct fetch" trio held across **all 40 backend + 53 frontend files** without exception. This pattern, locked in Planning §1.1, paid off when:

- Stage 5 could verify firewall integrity with a single `grep -L` per layer — confidence-scoring took minutes, not hours.
- Stage 7 build failure isolated to `useUsers.ts` because mutation hooks are the ONLY place TanStack mutation types appear. Fix was 3 edits, no ripple.

**For this stack, the layer firewall is more useful as a localisation tool than an architectural purity tool.**

## AC-11c self-collision was the right thing to lock

Planning §6.4 locked: "PUT same email to same user → 200, not 409." Without this, edits without email changes would 409 — visible UX failure on the second screen most users hit.

Both CodeGen and TestGen honoured it correctly because it was **explicitly named** in Gate-3 locks rather than left to the agent's judgement. The agent's default would have been "any IntegrityError → 409." This is the strongest argument in this run for locking decisions at the planning gate rather than discovering them at validation.

- **The codegen agent's instinct on shadcn was to hand-write primitives** rather than skip-or-error on the interactive `npx shadcn add`. That's correct (the published shadcn templates are stable + small enough to inline) but it required Stage 5 to spend a discrete check on "do these match canonical?" - **The self-review agent had no Write tool in its profile** — it returned the report content in chat and I materialised it. This is a tooling gap, not a model gap. Worth fixing in the agent definition before the next engagement.

## Highest-leverage speed-ups for THIS app shape (1-entity CRUD, bare HTML, PHP→FastAPI/React)

### 1. Pre-vendor a "Panasa CRUD starter" repo — saves ~60 min

The truly stack-stable artefacts in this engagement were:
- All 11 shadcn primitives (button, dialog, alert-dialog, form, table, input, label, skeleton, toast, toaster, use-toast)
- `tsconfig.json`, `vite.config.ts`, `vitest.config.ts`, `tailwind.config.ts`, `postcss.config.js`, `eslintrc.cjs`, `.prettierrc`, `components.json`
- Backend: `core/config.py`, `core/logging.py`, `db/base.py`, `db/engine.py`, `main.py` ProblemDetail handlers, `conftest.py`
- `Dockerfile` (backend + frontend), `docker-compose.yml`, `alembic.ini`, `pyproject.toml`, `requirements.txt`

These are **identical** for any 1-entity CRUD on this stack. The codegen agent reinvented all of them. **Cost: ~30 min of agent generation + risk of hand-written drift from canonical (the shadcn primitives concern from Gate 4 vanishes if they're vendored).**

CodeGen would only produce: `models.py`, `schemas.py`, `service.py`, `router.py`, `0001_<entity>.py` migration, `pages/<Entity>Page.tsx`, `components/<Entity>{DataTable,Form,AddEditDialog,DeleteAlertDialog}.tsx`, `lib/schemas.ts`, `api/<entity>.ts`, `hooks/use<Entity>.ts`, tests.

### 2. Ship the docker-compose template pre-fixed — saves ~40 min

All 8 dual-run fixes (`DR-1` through `DR-8`) were template-level mismatches:
- CORS env as JSON array literal
- Healthcheck path `/api/healthz`
- Env var name `CRUD_DATABASE_URL`
- PHP overlay host `mysql-legacy`
- Nginx upstream `fastapi-new`
- Playwright pip install in runner
- Seed emails using `.com`
- Frontend uses `VITE_API_BASE`

These are now-known bugs. Shipping the corrected template means Stage 7 goes from "build → fail → fix → rebuild → ..." to "build → smoke → done" in one pass.

### 3. Replace Discovery + Comprehension with one "extract spec" pass — saves ~75 min

For a 222-LOC, 1-entity, no-auth, no-framework app, the Discovery (12 BRs) + Comprehension (11 BR-Cs) outputs are **mechanical**. A human reading the 7 source files in 10 minutes produces the same spec. The two-stage Discovery → Comprehension split exists to handle multi-MWU enterprise apps; for trivially-shaped apps it's overkill.

A single "spec extraction" agent reading source/ and producing a 1-page contract (entity schema + 5 endpoints + 11 ACs + 4 risk flags) is enough. Skip Gate 1, keep Gate 2.

**Caveat:** this only works for apps where there's no surprise. For anything with non-trivial business rules (any FA module), keep both stages.

### 4. Generate Zod from OpenAPI — saves ~10 min + eliminates parity drift

OQ-P-001 deferred openapi-typescript codegen, but on this stack it's free speed. The Zod ↔ Pydantic message parity table (Planning §9.5) is mechanical — `openapi-typescript-codegen` or `kubb` produces both TypeScript types AND Zod schemas from the FastAPI `/openapi.json` endpoint at build time.

Stage 5 lost a check (parity verification) and Stage 6 lost a test class (Zod/Pydantic message divergence). For the next CRUD engagement, wire this in.

### 5. Skip the cockpit re-skin — saves ~90 min

The animated cockpit took ~90 minutes of polish (filling 28 TBDs, fixing 3 shorty references, rewriting STAGES array, etc.). For an internal demo or a sales conversation, **the 16-screenshot mosaic is the demo**. The cockpit is high-art but the customer's "aha" moment is the side-by-side mosaic + "we did this in 5 hours."

If you want the cockpit, generate it from a template that reads gate decisions + audit.jsonl + screenshots — turns a 90-min manual job into a 5-min render. The structure is fixed across engagements.

## Realistic floor — what's actually irreducible

With all 5 levers applied, the irreducible work for a chapagain-shaped app is:

| Block | Floor | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Spec extraction (1 agent run) | 15 min | Source still needs reading and the agent still thinks |
| Planning gate (HITL review of contract) | 10 min | Customer-specific decisions (email uniqueness? pagination?) still need a human |
| CodeGen (1 agent run, only ~12 logic files needed) | 15 min | Smaller surface → faster generation |
| Self-Review (1 agent run) | 10 min | |
| TestGen + run (1 agent run + pytest + vitest) | 15 min | Network + install is the floor |
| Dual-run (compose up + screenshot + smoke) | 10 min | Docker pulls + container starts |
| **Total** | **~75 min** | Plus ~15 min HITL across 3 remaining gates |

**Realistic floor for a 1-entity CRUD migration on this stack: ~90 min interactive.** That's a 3.3× speedup over the 5h I spent on this run.

## Mode B — Live screen capture (the sales-call companion)

When a salesperson is live-demoing on Zoom, a tiny background process records the screen (or browser tab) so they have a deliverable to send the prospect afterward. Options ranked by reliability:

| Tool | How | Pro | Con |
|---|---|---|---|

| **Loom / Tella / built-in QuickTime** | Manual click-to-record | Familiar to salespeople | Not integrated; we don't control the output |

  └─ for each token chunk:

Cockpit (HTML)
  └─ <pre> panel grows in real time → recorder sees every character

## Approach 1 — Live capture (what's happening while you work)

A tmux layout with the JSONL piped into a visible side pane, then record the whole tmux session.

```bash
# Pick the current session file (most-recently-modified .jsonl in this project's dir)
PROJ=~/.claude/projects/-Users-rahulchandra-01-Work-Projects-erplegacy-poc-2-FrontAccounting-master
SESSION=$(ls -t "$PROJ"/*.jsonl | head -1)

# Start a 2-pane tmux: claude on the left, JSONL tail on the right
tmux new-session -d -s claude-rec 'claude'
tmux split-window -t claude-rec -h "tail -F '$SESSION' | jq -r '...'"
asciinema rec --command 'tmux attach -t claude-rec' session.cast
```

The `jq` filter is the smart bit — it turns the raw JSONL into something readable. A starter:

```bash
jq -rc '
  if .type == "user" then "▸ USER: " + (.message.content // "" | tostring[0:120])
  elif .type == "assistant" then "● CLAUDE: " + ((.message.content[0].text // "") | tostring[0:120])
  elif .type == "assistant" and (.message.content[0].type == "tool_use") then "⚒  TOOL: " + .message.content[0].name + "(" + (.message.content[0].input | tostring[0:80]) + ")"
  elif .type == "user" and (.message.content[0].type == "tool_result") then "↩ RESULT: " + ((.message.content[0].content // "" | tostring)[0:120])
  else "· " + .type
  end
'
```

Result: side pane shows a running event stream in plain English. The recorder captures it because it's on screen.

**For background agents specifically:** their full transcript also gets written to:
```
/tmp/claude-501/<encoded-cwd>/<session-id>/tasks/<agent-id>.output
```
(The system warned me earlier not to read these from inside an agent context — they're huge JSONL transcripts of the subagent's whole conversation.)

A second tail can watch the tasks directory:
```bash

```

Stick that in a third tmux pane and you can literally watch background agents think while you're recording.

## Approach 2 — Post-hoc replay (render any past session)

Since the JSONL has everything, write it once and replay it forever. A small Python/Node tool that:
1. Reads the session JSONL
2. Renders each event to an HTML page with proper styling
3. Times the playback to either real-time (with original gaps) or compressed (e.g. "advance to next event every 2s")
4. Outputs an MP4 via Playwright recording the rendered page

This is the same Playwright pattern we discussed for the live-pipeline. Same recorder, different source feed.

**Strength:** you can replay any past session, including this one. The JSONL for our PNS-CRUD-001 work is on disk right now — we could turn it into a video tomorrow with no information loss.

## Approach 3 — Claude Code hooks (the structured route)

Claude Code supports settings-defined hooks that fire on `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `UserPromptSubmit`, etc. A `PostToolUse` hook can log every tool call (including agent spawns) to a structured file you control, with whatever formatting you want.

```jsonc
// ~/.claude/settings.json (or .claude/settings.local.json in your project)
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "*",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "jq -rc '\"[\\(now|strftime(\"%H:%M:%S\")) \\(.tool_name)]\"' >> ~/claude-recording.log"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Less flexible than tailing the JSONL directly, but gives you a clean, line-per-event log that's easier to render. Best used in *addition* to JSONL tailing, not instead of.

For the next time you want to record a Claude Code working session:

1. **Always:** the JSONL is already being written. Nothing to do.
2. **For live recording:** a tmux layout — main pane has Claude Code, right pane has the live JSONL pretty-tail, optional third pane has the background-agent tasks tail. Record with asciinema (small, replayable in HTML) or QuickTime (heavier, video file).
3. **For polished output:** post-process the JSONL with a renderer + Playwright. Same tool can re-render past sessions on demand.

The win is that approach 2 also works on **this session** retroactively — the JSONL is sitting on disk, we can build the renderer and the first asset it produces is "watch the PNS-CRUD-001 engagement unfold." No need to re-run anything.
